newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels may have softened conditions.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels may have softened conditions.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima may have softened their conditions for freeing the 83 hostages remaining in the mined and booby-trapped building.

In a communique read by one of the 20 hostages freed on Saturday, no mention was made of the condition the rebels stated after storming the residence on Dec. 17 -- the release of fellow members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement from Peruvian jails.
The communique said the hostage takers were willing "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."

"For (this) it is important to reflect why this extreme situation arose in the first place ... and to look at the situation in the prisons and the drama through which the families of our jailed comrades have lived for years.

"We think that this will allow it to be understood that our request should be attended to and thus permit in the long run .... a global and lasting peace. We will play a responsible role in that effort."
This wording was in marked contrast to a communique the guerrillas issued five days after they seized the residence during a reception to mark the birthday of Japanese emperor Akihito.

That communique said, "the liberation of the authorities which today are prisoners (inside the residence) will only be possible if the government arranges for the freedom of our members held in different prisons."
It was not clear if the hostage takers had actually dropped their main demand, which has been bluntly rejected by President Alberto Fujimori.
Since they seized the residence, the rebels have freed more than 420 hostages.
